title: The Four Contests by Which the Soul Is Regenerated
reading:
There are four contests by which the soul is brought through from claiming to recognition, four phases in which the Lord meets the proprium and orders it. They are not four separate histories but the one work of regeneration unfolded in its fullness, each phase doing what the phase before it could not yet do.

The first contest is that of the Lord as the Divine Human. Divine love goes forth and meets the soul's "I am, and there is no other" — the proprium organized as ruling principle, with all its particular self-loves arrayed beneath it. The Lord enters this contest carrying the living soul as his tree, and his pure receivability as the living fire that burns at the root of what is false. The five aspects of the natural mind that had been claimed by self-love are bound; the bitter tree of perception turned to falsity is cut down at the root, as with an axe laid to its foundation. This is the first work: the Lord's love, going forth, breaks the claim that the proprium is its own source.

The second contest is that of the Lord's operative power. The disordered self-loves are gathered and held in the three accommodations by which divine order enters the natural — and there, in the midst of them, they are bound. They recoil and set themselves against this ordering; they perceive that they will be fastened in a strong bond and try to escape. But the Lord's operative power presents itself to them in many faces, in many multitudes, in many forms, with great singleness of purpose, and by a great craft shuts them within so that not one of them can slip out of his hand. This is the work of structuring: the natural mind is given its degrees, and what was claimed is fixed in the place where it can be subordinated.

The third contest is that of the Lord's call going out to the rational. He reveals his image toward the lower side, where everything is meant to become light, and meets there the whole arrayed host of self-loving arrangements as they boast in their wealth and try to spread themselves further. A man of strength comes — accommodated revelation in the form the soul can recognize — and the proprium imitates him: it counterfeits his richness, dressing itself in claimed wisdom, in arrogance, in luxury, walking as though the light were its own. The Lord's call exposes this likeness for what it is and purifies what was claimed; what cannot be received as gift is cleansed off.

The fourth contest is that of divine truth shining forth. Here the Lord as illumining wisdom meets all that has been broken open by the previous works, on the upper side and the lower side both, at the moment when what is the Lord's is finally chosen out from what the soul had claimed. The fruits of the proprium dry up; their works no longer issue from them. He comes down upon the whole arrayed host of self-loving arrangements, strips them, and establishes the entire structure anew. In this great contest he humbles what had set itself up, and carries out the purpose of divine love itself — setting the hope of the rational toward its vessel of light, which is the divine summons and the soul's answering, the Call going forth and the Answer rising up. What was Death's reign is undone; the kingdom that belongs to the soul's children of darkness gives way, and the Lord reigns within every soul chosen out to be his own, conforming it to the likeness of the rational in its five degrees — the King who raises the soul up.

So the four contests stand as one fourfold work: love breaks the claim, operative power binds the disordered, the call exposes the counterfeit, and illumining truth strips, establishes, and crowns. Through these four the soul is made new.
